clue.text: This opening number is a star turn

definitions.meaning: 1 across is the first entry in the grid, and grid entries are called lights, so the first one leads them all
a prominent figure who outshines the rest of a company

explanation.surface: A compère announces that the show's first number is its headline act.
explanation.definitionFit: A pun on crossword lights for the first sense; the second is the idiom for the most prominent member of a group.

clue.text: Barge for setting the Thames on fire?

definitions.meaning: a flat-bottomed boat used to carry goods to and from ships

definitions.text: for setting the Thames on fire?
definitions.meaning: a device that makes a flame; 'set the Thames on fire' is a British idiom for doing something remarkable

explanation.surface: Someone wonders which river boat could make a spectacular impression on London.
explanation.definitionFit: A flat river boat for unloading cargo shares its name with a pocket device that makes a flame.

clue.text: East to follow odd lead from her

indicators.note: to follow means the letter for East comes after the rearranged letters
odd means strange or irregular, so the letters of lead are put in a new order

parts.note: E is the compass abbreviation for East

explanation.surface: A woman from the east takes a strange lead that others then follow.
explanation.walkthrough: 'odd' signals the anagram and 'to follow' places East after it. The definition 'her' is any woman, here one bearing this name.
explanation.definitionFit: A woman's given name, so a female person who could be referred to by the pronoun.

clue.text: Herein liquid refreshment for some writers

definitions.text: Herein liquid refreshment for some writers

parts.words: Herein liquid refreshment for some writers
parts.note: the 'refreshment' is not a drink but the dark fluid a pen is dipped in, kept on a desk holder for those who write

explanation.surface: A sign over a bar promises drinks for thirsty authors.
explanation.definitionFit: Desk holders for the fluid used by pens supply the 'drink' that writers' pens take up.

clue.text: Manner of walking in a crowd say

indicators.note: say means the word for the crowd is spoken, giving a word that sounds the same

parts.note: a gate is the number of spectators at a sports match

explanation.surface: Someone describes how a person moves when caught up in a throng.
explanation.walkthrough: GATE is British sporting usage for the attendance at a match; said aloud it sounds like the word for a way of walking.
explanation.definitionFit: A person's characteristic way of moving on foot, their stride or bearing.

clue.text: This strange fellow admits one to the Games

definitions.note: the clue's noun phrase stands for the adjective naming these ancient Greek games

indicators.note: strange signals that the letters of This are put into an unusual order
admits means the word for a fellow lets the letter for one inside it

parts.note: a fellow is a man
I is the Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: An odd man lets someone into the sporting contests.
explanation.walkthrough: 'strange' signals the anagram and 'admits' the container. The Isthmian Games were held at Corinth, so the adjective names those Games.
explanation.definitionFit: The ancient athletic festival held at the Corinthian isthmus in Greece was known by this adjective.

clue.text: Tory model in place of this beauty

definitions.text: Tory model in place of this beauty

parts.words: Tory model in place of this beauty
parts.note: a remodelled 'Tory' gives the name of the place this famous beauty belonged to, so she is the beauty 'of' that city in Greek legend

explanation.surface: A Conservative fashion model is replacing a pretty woman.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tory' rearranged gives TROY, the city whose legendary beauty launched a thousand ships; 'of this beauty' completes her title.
explanation.definitionFit: In Greek legend the most beautiful woman alive was carried off to the city of Troy, causing the Trojan War.

clue.text: Early English road maker according to GKC

definitions.text: Early English road maker according to GKC

parts.words: Early English road maker according to GKC
parts.note: Chesterton's poem The Rolling English Road says the winding roads were made by someone reeling home in drink

explanation.surface: A literary note on who built the first roads in England.
explanation.walkthrough: GKC is G K Chesterton, whose poem begins 'Before the Roman came to Rye ... The rolling English drunkard made the rolling English road'.
explanation.definitionFit: Chesterton blamed the winding English lanes on an intoxicated man staggering about, a habitual heavy drinker.

clue.text: Old garden theatre

definitions.meaning: the grove and garden in ancient Athens where Aristotle taught
a famous London playhouse in the West End

explanation.surface: A historic garden doubles as a playhouse.
explanation.definitionFit: Aristotle's school in Athens met in a sacred grove of that name, and a London West End playhouse borrowed it.

clue.text: For the present trouble in disguise

definitions.text: For the present trouble in disguise

parts.words: For the present trouble in disguise
parts.note: a present is a gift, and one that brings harm under a friendly appearance recalls the wooden horse left at Troy

explanation.surface: Something concealing a problem for now.
explanation.walkthrough: 'For the present' looks like 'for now', but it means 'as a gift'.
explanation.definitionFit: The wooden horse left by the Greeks at Troy is the classic example of a treacherous present.

clue.text: Form of conveyance from Tellson's Bank?

definitions.meaning: a goods vehicle, the British word for a truck
in Dickens's A Tale of Two Cities, Jarvis of that surname is a clerk at Tellson's Bank

explanation.surface: A banker asks about a way of transferring property.
explanation.walkthrough: 'conveyance' also suggests a legal transfer of property, which suits a bank.
explanation.definitionFit: A British truck carries goods, and Dickens named his Tellson's Bank clerk Jarvis with the same surname.

clue.text: Agreement in art yet to be worked out

indicators.note: worked out suggests solving a puzzle, and here the letters of art yet are rearranged into a new word

explanation.surface: A deal on an artwork is yet to be finalised.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to be worked out' rearranges ART YET.
explanation.definitionFit: A formal pact or accord between nations or parties.

clue.text: Importance of a summit

definitions.meaning: a peak or raised piece of ground

explanation.surface: The significance of a top-level meeting between leaders.
explanation.walkthrough: 'summit' looks like a political meeting, but it is a hilltop.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means both distinguished rank and a high piece of ground.

clue.text: Gypsy to see a chap about a chap

indicators.note: about means the first chap's name goes round the second word for a chap

parts.note: Roy is a man's name
a chap is a man

explanation.surface: A traveller goes to visit a man about another man.
explanation.walkthrough: 'about' signals the container; 'to see' is only padding linking the pieces, not part of the wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: A member of a travelling people, or their language, is called by this name.

clue.text: Night light for satellite broadcast

parts.note: Earth's natural satellite is the Moon
to beam is to transmit a signal

explanation.surface: A satellite transmission lights up the dark.
explanation.definitionFit: A ray of light reflected from the Moon shines at night.

clue.text: Boyfriend to hand bearing fruit

definitions.note: the phrase stands for a tree that bears fruit

parts.note: a date is someone you go out with
the palm is the inner surface of the hand

explanation.surface: A boyfriend offers a hand full of fruit.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is a little loose: 'bearing fruit' stands for the tree that bears dates.
explanation.definitionFit: A tall tropical tree that produces sweet brown fruits grown in desert oases.

clue.text: Move round two points on direction finder

indicators.note: on means the two compass points come first, placed on top of the word for the instrument in this down entry

parts.note: E and N are the compass points East and North
a compass shows which way is north

explanation.surface: Someone shifts position by a couple of degrees on a navigation instrument.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down entry 'on' puts EN above COMPASS.
explanation.definitionFit: To go around or surround something, enclosing it entirely.

clue.text: Strong man in Charles Dickens's fifth novel

indicators.note: novel means new or unusual, so these letters are made into a fresh arrangement
fifth picks out the letter in fifth place of the word Dickens

explanation.surface: A powerful character appears in the fifth book by Charles Dickens.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Dickens's fifth' is E, the fifth letter of DICKENS, and 'novel' rearranges CHARLES plus E. The surface wants a book title, but 'novel' is the anagram signal.
explanation.definitionFit: The Greek hero famed for his twelve labours is the classic mythological figure of great physical power.

clue.text: Move it closer in retreat

indicators.note: move means shift the letters of it closer into a different order

explanation.surface: Someone is told to push something nearer while withdrawing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Move' rearranges IT CLOSER.
explanation.definitionFit: A covered walk in a monastery, or a secluded religious house, is a place of withdrawal from the world.

clue.text: Repair shoes in the street

definitions.meaning: to mend footwear, as a shoemaker does
a rounded paving stone set in an old road

explanation.surface: A shoe mender works out on the pavement.
explanation.definitionFit: The verb is the shoemaker's mending, and the noun is a rounded stone used to pave old roads.

clue.text: Sour account by one returning hero

parts.note: I is the Roman numeral for one

indicators.note: returning means the hero's name comes back, read from right to left

parts.note: El Cid is the medieval Spanish hero

explanation.surface: A bitter tale is told of a hero coming home.
explanation.walkthrough: 'returning' applies only to the hero; El Cid is the eleventh-century Castilian warlord celebrated in Spanish epic.
explanation.definitionFit: Sharp and tart in taste, like vinegar or lemon juice.

clue.text: Having arrived as artists, they produce lots of pictures

parts.note: came is the past tense of arrive's synonym come
RA stands for Royal Academician, a member of Britain's Royal Academy of Arts, so artists are RAs

explanation.surface: Painters who have made it in the art world turn out many images.
explanation.walkthrough: 'as' only links the pieces. RA is Royal Academician, a member of the Royal Academy of Arts in London.
explanation.definitionFit: Devices for photography take many photographs or film footage.

clue.text: Certain changes made by Robert the Bruce?

parts.note: Bob is a short form of the name Robert
Robert the Bruce was King of Scots, so he was royal

explanation.surface: A historian asks what reforms the Scottish king introduced.
explanation.walkthrough: In bell-ringing a change is one ordering of the bells, and Bob Royal is a method rung on ten bells.
explanation.definitionFit: A bell-ringing method on ten bells, made up of successive orderings called changes.

clue.text: Patience typical of such works?

parts.note: Patience is a Gilbert and Sullivan comic piece, an example of musical stage works; the plural of opus is spelt the same

explanation.surface: Perseverance is characteristic of certain labours.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Patience' looks like the virtue but is the Gilbert and Sullivan piece; 'works' is also the Latin plural of opus.
explanation.definitionFit: Patience is an example of a sung stage drama, and the word is also the Latin plural of 'opus', meaning works.

clue.text: Assemble machine using this device

indicators.note: using signals that the answer is drawn from within the words assemble machine

explanation.surface: Instructions say to put together a machine with this gadget.
explanation.walkthrough: 'device' looks like a gadget, but it is the heraldic sense, a badge or symbol.
explanation.definitionFit: In heraldry a device is a symbolic badge or motif, the same thing as a symbol or badge.

clue.text: Turner portraying the French and English?

parts.note: la is French for the
the English word for the article is the

explanation.surface: A Turner painting depicts French and English scenes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Turner' suggests J M W Turner, the painter, but it is a machine that turns wood or metal.
explanation.definitionFit: A machine that turns wood or metal while a cutting tool shapes it.

clue.text: Small size in feet?

parts.note: a short unit of length, twelve of which make up a foot, so it is found in feet

explanation.surface: Someone asks about a small shoe size.
explanation.walkthrough: 'size in feet' suggests shoe size, but the small unit is part of a foot measurement.
explanation.definitionFit: A unit of length, one twelfth of a foot, so twelve sit inside each foot.

clue.text: "And summer's _____ hath all too short a date" (Shakespeare)

definitions.text: "And summer's _____ hath all too short a date" (Shakespeare)

parts.words: "And summer's _____ hath all too short a date" (Shakespeare)
parts.note: the blank is filled by the missing word from Sonnet 18, 'Shall I compare thee to a summer's day?', meaning a period of tenure

explanation.surface: A line from a Shakespeare sonnet with one word missing.
explanation.walkthrough: A fill-in-the-blank clue from Sonnet 18; the word means a rental term, so summer's time is short.
explanation.definitionFit: A contract granting use of property for a fixed term, used figuratively by Shakespeare for summer's allotted time.

clue.text: Fifteenth century House in the City

definitions.meaning: the royal dynasty that fought York in the Wars of the Roses
the county town of Lancashire in north-west England

explanation.surface: A medieval building stands in the financial district of London.
explanation.walkthrough: 'the City' suggests London's financial district, but it is a city in north-west England.
explanation.definitionFit: The red-rose royal dynasty of the Wars of the Roses took its name from the city in north-west England.

clue.text: The super feature of Tom but not Jerry

definitions.meaning: the British idiom for something excellent, the very best

definitions.text: feature of Tom but not Jerry
definitions.meaning: Tom and Jerry are the cartoon cat and mouse; only the cat has these facial bristles here

explanation.surface: A cartoon fan notes what the cat has that the mouse lacks.
explanation.walkthrough: 'the cat's whiskers' is a British idiom for the very best thing.
explanation.definitionFit: An idiom for something excellent, and literally the bristles on a feline's face, as on cartoon Tom.
